prompt: Which of these does a managed database service take off your hands?

choices.text: Replacing a failed disk and rebuilding the node
choices.why: Right. The machines and their failures sit below the shared-responsibility line.

choices.text: Choosing the shard key
choices.why: The shard key follows from your queries; the provider carries out whatever you pick.

choices.text: Deciding which operations need majority writes
choices.why: Write concern is a per-operation trade between latency and a guarantee, and it stays yours.

choices.text: Writing the retry after a failover drops a connection
choices.why: A failover still drops connections; retrying is the application's job.

prompt: A managed MongoDB promotes a new primary in a few seconds after a zone fails. What does the application still see?

choices.text: Dropped connections and errors on in-flight writes for those seconds
choices.why: Right. The provider builds the members; the application still retries and reconnects.

choices.text: Data loss, since managed services replicate asynchronously
choices.why: Majority-acknowledged writes survive an election wherever it is run.

choices.text: A maintenance window announced a week before
choices.why: A zone failure is not scheduled; maintenance windows are for patching.

choices.text: Nothing: managed failover is invisible to clients
choices.why: The election of lesson 9 still happens, with the same seconds of refused writes.

prompt: Why are major version upgrades of a managed database still started by the customer on most services?

choices.text: Providers are not allowed to install them under the licences
choices.why: The licences restrict who sells the service, not who runs an upgrade.

choices.text: A major upgrade deletes the backups taken on the old version
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says backups are deleted; the risk is the application's behaviour.

choices.text: Because they cost extra
choices.why: Price is not the reason given; behaviour is.

choices.text: They change behaviour the application depends on
choices.why: Right. Minor versions and OS patches are applied in your window; a major version needs testing by you first.

prompt: Match each product to a service run by the company that makes it.
A team moves its Redis to a managed plan with 1 GB of memory and `noeviction`. Six months later writes start failing with `OOM`. Whose problem is it, and what is the fix?

choices.text: The provider's: a managed service has to scale memory by itself
choices.why: Every plan has a size; reaching it is a capacity decision above the line.

choices.text: The team's: a larger plan or less data, and a bigger invoice either way
choices.why: Right. It looks exactly like lessons 14 and 20; only the fix is a plan instead of a VM.

choices.text: Nobody's: switching to `allkeys-lru` fixes it at no cost
choices.why: Under eviction, data is deleted; whether that is free depends on whether Redis is a cache or the database.

choices.text: The provider's, because `OOM` is a crash of their server
choices.why: Redis stays up and refuses writes; nothing crashed.

prompt: A managed MongoDB accepts a shard key that sends every new order to one shard. Why will this not appear on the provider's status page?

choices.text: It is a decision about the data, carried out exactly as made
choices.why: Right. The service works as designed; the design was yours.

choices.text: Status pages only cover Redis and Cassandra
choices.why: Every provider has one, for every service; this is just not something it covers.

choices.text: The balancer of lesson 10 will fix it within the hour
choices.why: The balancer moves chunks; it cannot spread writes that all land on the newest key range.

choices.text: The provider hides incidents caused by sharding
choices.why: Nothing is hidden; there is no incident on their side to report.

prompt: Why is a table that reads a thousand tombstones to return ten rows worse on a service that charges per read than on your own hardware?

choices.text: Providers keep tombstones forever
choices.why: Compaction still removes them after the grace period.

choices.text: It is not worse: the provider absorbs the extra work
choices.why: The extra work is what the per-read price measures.

choices.text: There, every wasted read is billed
choices.why: Right. Almost every axis of a managed service is billed, so a modelling mistake becomes a monthly cost.

choices.text: Managed services refuse reads with tombstones
choices.why: They apply the same thresholds you choose; refusal is not the difference.

prompt: Which of these does a restore drill on a managed service answer that its documentation does not? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Which licence the database is under
choices.why: A licence is read in a file or an announcement, not found by restoring.

choices.text: How long a restore of your actual data takes
choices.why: Right: the number that goes into the runbook and the exit plan.

choices.text: What the restored copy is missing, such as users or settings outside the data
choices.why: Right: found in a drill rather than in an incident.

choices.text: Who in the team knows where the button is
choices.why: Right: a restore nobody knows how to start takes longer than any documentation says.

prompt: Which of these keeps a managed database private?

choices.text: A long password shared by every application
choices.why: One shared password means one leak opens every door.

choices.text: Private network only, TLS, one account per app
choices.why: Right: the three settings every provider has under different names.

choices.text: Trusting the provider's audit log to block intruders
choices.why: A log records who connected; it blocks nobody, and reading it is yours.

choices.text: A public endpoint on a port other than the default
choices.why: A different port hides nothing from a scanner.

prompt: A backup that nobody has ever ___ is a hope, whoever took it.
Amazon DocumentDB answers MongoDB drivers. What is the first document to read before moving an application to it?

choices.text: The SSPL, to check it may be used
choices.why: Using a service for your own application is not what the SSPL restricts.

choices.text: The pricing page
choices.why: Price matters, but it says nothing about which of your queries will work.

choices.text: MongoDB's own manual, since the engine is the same
choices.why: It is a different engine behind a translation layer.

choices.text: Its list of unsupported features
choices.why: Right. What is missing from the translation is found there or in production.

prompt: Match each product to its licence situation.

pairs.right: RSALv2 or SSPLv1, a dual licence

prompt: The lab searched the `redis:7.4` image for a licence file and found none. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: Redis 7.4 is still BSD-licensed, since nothing says otherwise
choices.why: A missing file says nothing about the licence; Redis announced the change for 7.4.

choices.text: It rests on what Redis announced
choices.why: Right. The lab confirms version 7.4.11 and cannot confirm the licence; the lesson says which is which.

choices.text: The image is Valkey under another name
choices.why: `redis-server --version` printed Redis 7.4.11.

choices.text: The image cannot be legally run
choices.why: Running Redis for your own application is allowed under every licence discussed.

prompt: A shop stores its sessions in self-hosted Redis 7.4 and sells shoes, not databases. What does the RSALv2/SSPLv1 change mean for it today?

choices.text: It has to move to Valkey before the next upgrade
choices.why: Nothing forces it; Valkey is one option among several.

choices.text: Nothing for its own use; it matters for which providers and versions are on offer to it later
choices.why: Right. The restriction is on selling Redis as a service; the shop's future choices are what change.

choices.text: It owes Redis a licence fee
choices.why: Neither licence charges a fee for running the software yourself.

choices.text: It has to publish its application's source code
choices.why: That obligation is about offering the database itself as a service.

prompt: Valkey was forked from Redis version ___, the last release under the BSD licence.
A dump reads at 50 MB/s. How many hours does it take to read 1 TB (1,000,000 MB)? Round to one decimal place.
Why does the lesson call features beyond the database, such as built-in search or triggers, the cost that hides?

choices.text: They are billed separately and nobody reads that part of the invoice
choices.why: The hidden cost is the work of replacing them, not their price.

choices.text: Each must be rebuilt elsewhere on leaving
choices.why: Right. Listing them as they are adopted keeps the exit priced.

choices.text: They slow the database down
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; leaving is.

choices.text: They break the licence of the database
choices.why: A provider's own features are under its terms, not the database's licence.

prompt: A shop cannot close for a night, and its dump-and-restore takes nine hours. Which exit route fits?

choices.text: Replicate continuously into the new place and switch over in minutes
choices.why: Right, and it is a project of its own, which is why it is priced early.

choices.text: Ask the provider to export faster
choices.why: The export speed is the provider's; the window is still yours to fit.

choices.text: Stay, since leaving is impossible
choices.why: Leaving costs a project, which is a price, not an impossibility.

choices.text: Dump and restore anyway, with writes allowed during the dump
choices.why: Writes after the dump are lost on the new side.

prompt: What does restoring the provider's exported backup into your own containers prove that no other exit test does?

choices.text: That the provider's features exist outside
choices.why: A data restore does not bring search indexes or triggers with it.

choices.text: That the licence permits leaving
choices.why: No licence here restricts leaving.

choices.text: That egress will be free
choices.why: A restore says nothing about transfer prices.

choices.text: That your own software reads it, and how fast
choices.why: Right: the three things the section lists.

prompt: Which decision stays with you on every managed service, whatever the provider's tier?

choices.text: Which zone the replacement node is built in
choices.why: Rebuilding failed nodes is the provider's work.

choices.text: When the operating system of the nodes is patched
choices.why: You choose a window; the provider patches.

choices.text: How backups are stored durably
choices.why: Storage of backups is below the line.

choices.text: Whether reads go to a secondary
choices.why: Right. Read preference is a per-operation trade only you are in a position to judge.

prompt: Order an exit test, from first to last.
items: Export the provider's backup to storage you control
Start containers of the same product in your lab
Run the application's reads against the copy
Write the time it all took into the exit plan
trap: You cannot restore what you have not exported, nor time what has not finished.

prompt: A Cassandra-compatible service passes all of an application's tests. What can still differ from the Cassandra of lessons 16 to 19?

choices.text: How it behaves under load
choices.why: Right. The engine underneath is the provider's own.

choices.text: The licence of the driver
choices.why: The driver is the same one; the engine is what changed.

choices.text: The data types, which are always translated to JSON
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the difference named is the engine.

choices.text: The CQL syntax of the queries that passed
choices.why: Those queries passed; the syntax they used is accepted.
